GAGA theorem

Words: 55
Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
For a projective variety over the complex numbers, analytification gives an equivalence between algebraic and analytic coherent sheaves, preserves their cohomology, and is fully faithful on their morphisms. In particular, a holomorphic isomorphism between algebraic line bundles is algebraic. This allows a complex-torus proof of a line-bundle identity to establish the corresponding algebraic identity on a projective elliptic curve.

Very general point of an algebraic parameter space

Words: 50
Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
A property holds at a very general point of an irreducible complex algebraic parameter space if it holds outside a countable union of proper Zariski-closed subsets. This permits countably many exceptional conditions. Over C that complement is nonempty and dense, for example by the Baire category theorem on a local smooth analytic chart.

Hilbert scheme (HilbP(X))

Words: 513 Articles: 8
Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
For a projective scheme X and a fixed Hilbert polynomial P, the Hilbert scheme parametrizes flat families of closed subschemes of X with that polynomial. This turns a family of embedded algebraic curves into an algebraic parameter space.

Hilbert functor (HilbX/k​)

Words: 203 Articles: 2
Hilbert scheme OurBigBook.com
For a projective scheme X over a field k, the Hilbert functor assigns to a k-scheme T the set of closed subschemes W⊆X×k​T which are of finite presentation, proper and flat over T. Pullback of families makes it a contravariant functor. After choosing a very ample line bundle, requiring a fixed fibre Hilbert polynomial P gives the subfunctor represented by HilbP(X). The unrestricted functor is represented by the disjoint union of these Hilbert schemes.

Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
Étale cohomology is sheaf cohomology on the site whose objects are étale morphisms Y→X and whose coverings are jointly surjective families of such morphisms. Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
An algebraic set is a zero locus of polynomial equations, allowing reducible sets. An affine algebraic set uses ordinary polynomial equations; a projective algebraic set uses homogeneous equations in projective coordinates. On affine or projective space, closed sets in the Zariski topology are algebraic sets, and an irreducible algebraic set is an algebraic variety in the classical convention.

Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
An abelian variety of dimension g has complex multiplication when its rational endomorphism ring contains a commutative semisimple Q-algebra of dimension 2g. For an elliptic curve in characteristic zero, this means its geometric endomorphism ring of an elliptic curve is an order in an imaginary quadratic field. The resulting rank-one Tate module representations connect torsion points to class field theory.

A complex CM period compares an algebraic invariant differential on a CM elliptic curve with its analytic lattice coordinate. At an ordinary prime, a p-adic CM period compares the same differential with the invariant differential of the multiplicative formal group: an isomorphism η is normalized by logE​η(T)=Ωp​log(1+T). Matched periods make normalized critical Hecke L-function values algebraic and give precise p-adic L-function interpolation.

For a complex CM torus C/a and an idele s of its CM field, the automorphism corresponding to s by Artin reciprocity takes its lattice to s−1a and acts on torsion through the adelic scalar s−1. Comparison with the original curve gives a scalar in the CM field, producing the Hecke character of a CM elliptic curve.

A subset of an algebraic variety is Zariski dense when its closure in the Zariski topology is the whole variety. For an affine variety, this is equivalent to saying that every regular function vanishing on the subset vanishes on the entire variety.

A linear system of divisors is a projective family of effective Weil divisors linearly equivalent to a fixed divisor. For a Cartier divisor, the family is obtained from global sections of its associated line bundle. The algebraic curve case recovers the usual moving family of effective divisors.

On a smooth projective curve of genus two, D=K+P+Q has three sections and no base points by the Riemann-Roch theorem. Its map to P2 is nondegenerate and has mapping degree times image degree four. The only nonbirational possibility is a double cover of a conic. Every degree-two divisor with two sections is canonical, again by Riemann-Roch theorem, so that possibility forces D∼2K, or P+Q∼K. If this equivalence fails, the image is a quartic and the map is birational. The quartic is singular because a smooth plane quartic has genus three.

An algebraic variety is a geometric space locally described by polynomial equations, together with its regular functions.

Algebraic variety OurBigBook.com
A rational map is a morphism of algebraic varieties defined on a dense open subset, with representatives identified when they agree on a smaller dense open subset. For an integral source and a separated variety as target, agreement on a dense open determines a morphism uniquely. This definition also permits nonprojective sources.

Algebraic variety OurBigBook.com
For a possibly reducible algebraic variety X, take pairs (U,f) with U a dense open subset and f a regular function on U. Identify pairs agreeing on a common dense open subset. Addition and multiplication on intersections make these classes a ring. For an affine variety with reduced coordinate ring A, this ring is its total quotient ring. For an irreducible variety, it is the function field. An isomorphism of dense open subsets induces an isomorphism of these rings.

Words: 83
Ring of rational functions on a reduced variety OurBigBook.com
Let Y be the reduced union of the irreducible components of an affine variety X containing P. Removing all other components leaves an open neighbourhood of P on which X and Y agree, so their local rings at P agree. In the coordinate ring B=k[Y], every denominator not vanishing at P avoids all minimal primes: each component of Y contains P. Such a denominator is a non-zero-divisor. Consequently BmP​​ injects into the total quotient ring Q(B)=Rat(Y). One cannot generally replace Y by a single component through an intersection point.

A locally closed affine algebraic set in a projective space, equivalently an open subset of a closed subset of projective space cut out by homogeneous polynomials. Reducibility is allowed for an algebraic set; an irreducible variety with such an embedding is a quasi-projective variety.

An irreducible variety which admits a locally closed embedding into projective space. Open subsets of affine varieties and blowups of algebraic varieties along closed centres give important examples.

An algebraic variety whose underlying topological space with its Zariski topology is an irreducible topological space: it is nonempty and cannot be a union of two proper closed subsets. For a reduced affine variety, this is equivalent to its coordinate ring being an integral domain.

A constructible subset is a finite union of locally closed subsets in the Zariski topology. A dense constructible subset contains a dense open subset. Constructibility alone is weaker than closedness, but a constructible subgroup is closed.

Algebraic variety OurBigBook.com
For an algebraic variety X defined over a field K, a K-rational point is a morphism SpecK→X over K. In affine coordinates it is a solution of the defining equations with every coordinate in K; in projective coordinates it is a nonzero coordinate vector over K, considered up to common nonzero scaling. The set is denoted X(K). Over a number field, having points over every completion need not imply having a rational point; for genus-one coverings this failure is recorded by the Tate–Shafarevich group.

An algebraic variety is smooth over its ground field when its structural morphism is smooth. Over an algebraically closed field its local rings are regular; on an irreducible variety its tangent spaces all have the variety's dimension of a scheme.

Over a perfect field, a point of an algebraic variety is smooth exactly when its local ring is a regular local ring. The smooth locus of a variety is open; its closed complement is the singular locus.

The normalization of an integral algebraic variety is obtained by taking the integral closure of its affine coordinate rings in its function field. An algebraic curve is a one-dimensional algebraic variety. On a smooth algebraic curve, the local ring at every closed point is a discrete valuation ring, which allows orders of zeros and poles to be recorded as a divisor on an algebraic curve.

Its Zariski tangent space has dimension one, and a local coordinate can be chosen in the direction of a nonzero partial derivative. A smooth algebraic curve has all points nonsingular. Over a complete local field, the Hensel lemma lifts a nonsingular residue point by solving for a coordinate with unit partial derivative.

Algebraic curve OurBigBook.com
An affine algebraic curve is an affine variety of Krull dimension one. An irreducible affine curve has a finitely generated one-dimensional domain as its coordinate ring. Quotienting this ring by a nonzero element gives a zero-dimensional Noetherian ring, hence an Artinian ring. Consequently a nonzero regular function has finitely many zeros. No nonsingularity assumption is part of the definition.

Its affine version y2=z3, used below, differs only by renaming a coordinate. At the point [0:1:0], the chart y=1 gives z=x3, which is smooth and exhibits its unique smooth flex of a cuspidal cubic.

For D={y2z=x3}, the determinant of the homogeneous Hessian matrix is 24xy2. Its intersections with D are the cusp [0:0:1] and the smooth point [0:1:0]. The Hessian criterion for a flex therefore gives a unique smooth flex, with tangent z=0 and contact order three. Consequently every pair consisting of a triple line and a cuspidal cubic meeting only at a smooth point is projectively equivalent to (3{z=0},D).

The kernel of x↦t3, y↦t4, z↦t5 is generated by y2−xz, yz−x3, z2−x2y. The adjugate matrix is a nonzero multiple of vvT, so the determinant has a simple zero. At rank at most one, the projective kernel contains a line and the quadratic vTM′v has a zero on it; that point would make the total surface singular. Thus every singular fibre is a pair of distinct projective lines and its discriminant zero is simple.

A k-algebra isomorphism between the local rings at closed points extends to a morphism on some neighborhoods: represent the images of finitely many affine coordinate generators by fractions, and shrink where their denominators are nonzero and their finitely many relations hold. Taking inverse images of these neighborhoods then gives mutually inverse actual neighborhood isomorphisms, not just a formal-completion isomorphism.

Bézout's theorem OurBigBook.com
For projective plane curves without a common irreducible component, project from a point outside both curves. In coordinates where that point is [1:0:0], their defining homogeneous polynomials have constant nonzero leading coefficients in X. The resultant in X is nonzero by Gauss's lemma, and is homogeneous of degree degCdegD in the remaining two coordinates. Every intersection projects to one of its zeros. Each projection line has only finitely many intersections with the curves, so their intersection is finite. Choose the center again outside all joining lines of pairs of intersection points; the projection is now injective on that finite set, proving the bound.

Let two triples of projective lines meet in nine distinct points. Any plane cubic containing eight contains all nine. Overlapping nine-point configurations then force each next point onto the same cubic by eight-point cubic completion for two triples of lines. A unibranch singular point of an algebraic variety on a plane algebraic curve. The ordinary cusp has local equation y2=x3 and parametrization (x,y)=(t2,t3); its branch has a repeated tangent and a vanishing first derivative at the singular point. Higher-order cusps may have different local equations. A cuspidal cubic gives the basic projective example.

Singular point of an algebraic variety OurBigBook.com
A point on F=0 where all first partial derivatives vanish. For a reduced hypersurface this is the Jacobian criterion; a nondegenerate quadratic leading part defines an ordinary double point.
Secant line through singular points of a cubic hypersurface
Words: 61
Hypersurface singularity OurBigBook.com
Restrict a cubic equation to the affine line through two distinct singular points. At each point the equation and its first directional derivative vanish, so the restricted polynomial has two distinct double roots. A polynomial of degree at most three with this property is identically zero. Hence the whole line lies in the hypersurface. The multiplicity argument works in every characteristic.
Ordinary double point
Words: 48
Singular point of an algebraic variety OurBigBook.com
For a reduced plane algebraic curve, an ordinary double point is a point whose lowest nonzero local homogeneous term has degree 2 and factors into two distinct linear factors over an algebraic closure. The two factors give distinct tangent directions. In characteristic not 2, x2+y2+higher terms is an example.

Smooth locus of a variety OurBigBook.com
If X⊆An is irreducible of dimension d, choose a nonzero (n−d)-rowed minor of a Jacobian matrix at one point of minimum tangent dimension. Closed-point dimension lemma for affine domains (dimAm​=dimA)

Words: 152 Articles: 1
Krull dimension of an affine variety OurBigBook.com
If A is a finite-type integral domain over an algebraically closed field and dimA=d, every maximal ideal m has height of a prime ideal d. Choose a Noether normalization k[z1​,…,zd​]⊂A. The contraction of m is a maximal ideal of the polynomial ring and has height d; going-down theorem lifts its full chain since the polynomial ring is integrally closed domain. The upper bound is dimA. A principal open subset containing a closed point consequently has dimension d, because the whole chain under that point survives localization.

Closed-point dimension lemma for affine domains OurBigBook.com
For an irreducible variety which is an affine variety of dimension d and a nonzero nonunit regular function f, each irreducible component of V(f) has dimension d−1. Choose a closed point on just the component in question. In its local ring R, (f)​ is that component's prime ideal. A system of parameters of R/(f), lifted and supplemented by f, generates a maximal-primary ideal; the Krull height theorem gives dimR/(f)≥d−1. Extending any chain above (f) by the zero prime of the domain gives the reverse inequality. This proof does not identify dimension with transcendence degree.

Smooth point on an irreducible hypersurface in positive characteristic

Words: 74
Affine hypersurface OurBigBook.com
Let k be algebraically closed of characteristic p>0 and let f∈k[x1​,…,xn​] be irreducible. Some partial derivative of f is nonzero: otherwise every exponent is divisible by p, and perfection of k would make f a pth power. If the gradient vanished at every point of Z(f), the Strong Hilbert Nullstellensatz would put each partial derivative in (f), impossible by degree. Hence Z(f) has a smooth point and minimum tangent dimension n−1.

Projective hypersurface OurBigBook.com
Over the complex numbers the displayed projective plane curve has precisely two singular points, [1:0:1] and [−1:0:1]. At either, with X=±1+u, Y=v, Z=1, the leading quadratic term is 4u2±v2, so they are ordinary double points. The derivative equations in the chart Y=1 have no solution: writing d=X2−Z2 forces both d2=−1/16 and d2=1. Principality criterion on a complex elliptic curve (∑nP​[P] principal⟺∑nP​=0 and ∑nP​P=0 in E)

Words: 88
Principal divisor on an algebraic curve OurBigBook.com
For E=C/Λ, integrate the logarithmic derivative of an elliptic function and its product with z around a fundamental cell. The first integral forces total degree zero; the second forces the weighted point sum to lie in the lattice. Conversely choose lifts of the points with equal zero and pole sums, and form the balanced ratio of translated Weierstrass sigma functions. Their quasi-period factors cancel, giving an elliptic function with exactly the prescribed divisor. Separate zero and pole divisors require disjoint support; common terms cancel when only their difference is prescribed.

Intersection dimension bound on a smooth variety (dim(Y∩Z)j​≥dimY+dimZ−dimX)

Words: 60
Intersection theory OurBigBook.com
For closed irreducible subvarieties Y,Z of a smooth d-dimensional algebraic variety X, every irreducible component of their intersection has dimension at least dimY+dimZ−d. Locally the diagonal of X×X is cut out by d parameters. Intersecting it with Y×Z and applying the Krull height theorem gives the bound. The three-dimensional affine quadric cone shows that the same lower bound can fail when X is singular.

Successive intersection with Cartier divisors gives a cycle class. On an n-dimensional complete scheme, its degree is multilinear and depends only on numerical divisor classes; the top product with one divisor is its self-intersection number.

For a proper morphism of varieties f:X→Y, a Cartier divisor D on Y, and an algebraic cycle α on X, pullback of D, intersection with α, and proper pushforward satisfy the displayed identity in the Chow group. Words: 102 Articles: 1
Chow group OurBigBook.com
For a smooth complex projective algebraic variety, the cycle class map sends an algebraic cycle of codimension r to the Poincare dual of its homology class. Rational equivalence gives the same cohomology class, so the map descends to the Chow group. It respects intersection products, pullback and proper pushforward; a cohomological obstruction therefore obstructs the corresponding proposed identity of Chow classes.

The map factors through the Chow group, but a Chow class retains finer information than its cohomological cycle class.

External product of Chow classes OurBigBook.com
On E×E for a complex elliptic curve, the two factor curves and the diagonal have intersection matrix ​011​101​110​​, of determinant two. Their cohomology classes are therefore independent. The degree-one image of the external product of Chow classes has cohomology contained in the span of the two factor classes. The cycle class map thus shows that the diagonal is outside that image, proving failure of surjectivity.

Chern class axioms in the Chow ring (ci​(E)∈CHi(X))

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Chern class OurBigBook.com
For a vector bundle E of rank r on a smooth algebraic variety, algebraic Chern classes have c0​(E)=1, vanish for i>r, commute with pullback, and obey the Whitney sum formula for Chern classes for every short exact sequence of vector bundles. A line bundle O(D) has total class 1+[D]. The projective-bundle splitting construction makes pullback injective and supplies a filtration by line bundles, so these axioms determine all classes as elementary symmetric functions of their first classes. In particular, ci​(E∗)=(−1)ici​(E) and c1​(L⊗M)=c1​(L)+c1​(M) in the ordinary Chow ring.

Chern class in complex cobordism (cjMU​(E)∈MU2j(X))

Words: 124 Articles: 1
Chern class OurBigBook.com
The complex orientation of complex cobordism defines Chern classes of actual complex bundles by the splitting principle and elementary symmetric expressions in the first Chern classes of line summands. For an actual rank-n complex bundle, its top Chern class is its Euler class in a generalized cohomology theory. Chern classes extend stably by the Whitney formula; this stable extension must not be confused with the Euler class of a merely stably complex real bundle.

Chern number (⟨ci1​​⋯cis​​,[M]⟩)

Words: 53
Chern class OurBigBook.com
On a compact oriented 2r-manifold without boundary, an integral product of Chern classes of total complex degree r pairs with the fundamental class to give a Chern number. A unitary connection supplies Chern-Weil theory representatives, but the integer is independent of that connection. The Second Chern number on a four-manifold is one important example; the integral of the First Chern class over a closed surface is another.

For a rank-r complex vector bundle, let h=c1​(S∗) for the tautological line S on its projective bundle. The Leray-Hirsch theorem gives the free basis 1,h,…,hr−1 over base cohomology. These derivatives define a derivation with values in O(−1)⊕(n+1), hence a map from the Kähler differential sheaf. The last map is (gi​)↦∑i​Xi​gi​. On Xi​=0, put yj​=Xj​/Xi​ and use frame Xi−1​. The derivative of yj​ has coordinate vector with 1 at j, −yj​ at i and zero elsewhere. Those vectors form a free basis of the kernel of (bi​)↦bi​+∑j=i​yj​bj​, proving exactness directly in every characteristic.
